cx-b1-sign-in-first-task.q: Why does the lesson recommend signing in to Codex with your ChatGPT account rather than an API key for typical use?
options: API keys are inherently less secure than ChatGPT sign-in
It draws usage from your existing ChatGPT plan's rolling 5-hour window instead of billing per token on a separate developer account
API keys are not supported by the Codex CLI at all
There is no practical difference between the two options
cx-b1-sign-in-first-task.why: Signing in with ChatGPT bills against your plan's shared usage window, while an API key bills per token against a separate account - a common early mistake is not realizing this before racking up token charges.

cx-b1-sign-in-first-task.q: What's the recommended approval mode for your very first Codex session in a project?
options: Full-access/auto-approve mode, to see everything Codex can do immediately
Disable all approval prompts to move faster
A conservative mode like read-only or 'suggest,' so changes are proposed before anything is written
There is no approval mode setting to configure
cx-b1-sign-in-first-task.why: Starting in a conservative mode lets Codex propose changes without writing files until you approve, which is how you learn its behavior before trusting it with real, unreviewed edits.

cx-b1-sign-in-first-task.q: The example first-task prompt explicitly says 'do not modify or delete any existing files.' Why include that guardrail on a first task?
options: It evaluates Codex's judgment on something low-risk while you're still learning how it behaves
It's a hard technical limitation - Codex literally cannot delete files
Codex cannot create new files without this instruction
It's unnecessary boilerplate with no real effect
cx-b1-sign-in-first-task.why: A narrow, low-risk first task with an explicit guardrail against touching existing files lets you evaluate Codex's judgment safely before delegating anything higher-stakes.

cx-b2-understand-a-repository.q: Why does the lesson insist on exploring a new repository in read-only mode before any edit task?
options: Read-only mode runs noticeably faster than edit mode
It prevents changes based on a wrong mental model - you verify your understanding before trusting it enough to edit
Codex cannot technically explore and edit in the same session
It's required to display the directory structure at all
cx-b2-understand-a-repository.why: Doing exploration in read-only mode first, before any edit task, prevents changes based on a wrong mental model of the codebase.

cx-b2-understand-a-repository.q: Codex gives you a repo tour with cited file paths. What should you do before trusting the whole summary?
options: Nothing further - Codex's citations are inherently accurate
Open at least two of the cited files yourself to confirm they say what Codex claims
Ask a colleague to independently redo the same tour
Immediately have Codex begin editing based on the tour
cx-b2-understand-a-repository.why: Trusting the summary without opening any cited file is listed as a common mistake - spot-checking two files takes a minute and confirms the claims are grounded in the real code.

cx-b2-understand-a-repository.q: The repository you're exploring has no AGENTS.md file. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Skip it entirely - AGENTS.md is optional and rarely provides real value
Copy an AGENTS.md from an unrelated project as a starting point
Ask Codex to draft one based only on what it found in the repo, then review and edit it yourself before committing
Write one from scratch without involving Codex at all
cx-b2-understand-a-repository.why: The lesson treats the exploration session as the ideal moment to draft an AGENTS.md from what was actually found - but warns not to accept it unread.

cx-b3-writing-specs-for-agents.q: Which of these is written as a checkable acceptance criterion, per the lesson's spec template?
options: "User sees an error message if the field is empty"
"Better UX for the search feature"
"Clean, maintainable code"
"Search should feel intuitive"
cx-b3-writing-specs-for-agents.why: The lesson warns against writing criteria as adjectives ('better UX', 'clean', 'intuitive') and requires specific, checkable statements instead.

cx-b3-writing-specs-for-agents.q: Why does the spec template include explicit constraints and non-goals, like 'do not add a new backend endpoint'?
options: It's required formatting for Codex to parse the spec
It prevents the agent from 'helpfully' touching unrelated code or adding infrastructure you didn't ask for
It makes the spec appear more professional to reviewers
It replaces the need to write acceptance criteria
cx-b3-writing-specs-for-agents.why: Omitting constraints and non-goals is listed as a common mistake because it lets the agent scope-creep into unrelated code or unwanted infrastructure.

cx-b3-writing-specs-for-agents.q: Per the lesson's proTip, what's the difference between a task spec and an AGENTS.md file?
options: They serve exactly the same purpose and can be used interchangeably
A spec is task-specific; AGENTS.md is standing, repo-wide context that applies to every future task
AGENTS.md fully replaces the need for writing specs
Specs are for bug fixes only, and AGENTS.md is for features only
cx-b3-writing-specs-for-agents.why: The proTip draws a clean line: anything true for every future task belongs in AGENTS.md so you stop repeating it in every individual spec.

cx-i1-implement-a-feature.q: Why does the workflow require Codex to present an implementation plan before writing any code?
options: It's a formality with little practical benefit
Codex technically cannot generate code without a written plan first
It catches a wrong architectural choice, like violating a stated constraint, before any code exists - far cheaper to fix at that point
Plans are only useful for large, multi-week features
cx-i1-implement-a-feature.why: The plan-first checkpoint catches problems like proposing a new database table when a constraint forbids it, while it's still cheap to redirect.

cx-i1-implement-a-feature.q: Codex reports 'all tests pass' after implementing a feature. What should you do next?
options: Accept the claim and merge, since Codex ran the command
Ask for the actual, pasted command output - not just the claim
Assume it's true and move on to the next task
Re-run the tests yourself silently, without telling Codex
cx-i1-implement-a-feature.why: Accepting 'tests pass' as a claim instead of asking for actual command output is listed as a common mistake - the pasted output closes the gap between claim and demonstrated fact.

cx-i1-implement-a-feature.q: For a genuinely hard or ambiguous implementation task, what does the lesson's proTip suggest?
options: Simply implement whichever approach Codex proposes first
Skip the planning step entirely to save time
Always send it to a cloud task instead of working locally
Ask Codex to try more than one approach and compare trade-offs before committing to a full implementation
cx-i1-implement-a-feature.why: Comparing approaches before committing is cheaper than discovering the wrong one only after a full implementation has already been built.

cx-i2-debug-a-failing-build.q: Why does the debugging prompt require pasting the full error output and stack trace instead of a paraphrase?
options: Paraphrasing violates Codex's terms of service
A paraphrase forces Codex to guess at context it actually needs to diagnose the failure correctly
Full stack traces are technically required before Codex will start any session
It makes no real difference either way
cx-i2-debug-a-failing-build.why: Pasting only the error message instead of the full trace is a listed common mistake - it forces Codex to guess at details it needs for an accurate diagnosis.

cx-i2-debug-a-failing-build.q: Codex proposes wrapping the failing code in a try/catch that swallows the error, and the test now passes. How should this be judged?
options: This is a valid, acceptable minimal fix
It's fine as long as the overall suite is green afterward
This fixes the symptom, not the bug, and can quietly reintroduce the same failure later - the root cause must be verified first
This is the fastest and therefore preferred approach
cx-i2-debug-a-failing-build.why: The lesson warns that under pressure to 'just make it pass,' an agent may take the fastest route rather than fixing the actual root cause - which is why hypothesis verification comes before any fix.

cx-i2-debug-a-failing-build.q: If a fix genuinely requires changing an existing test, what should Codex be asked to do?
options: Change it silently so the diff stays small and clean
Explain the old expectation and why the new one is correct, ideally recorded in the commit message
Delete the test file entirely rather than modify it
Skip the test with a TODO comment and revisit it later
cx-i2-debug-a-failing-build.why: The proTip says the reasoning behind a legitimate test change should be documented in the commit message, not just chat, so it survives for the next reviewer.

cx-i3-code-review-with-codex.q: A Codex review comment flags a variable naming inconsistency that your linter already enforces. What should you do?
options: Fix it anyway, since Codex specifically flagged it
Tell Codex to skip style/formatting comments already enforced by the linter, and focus on correctness, security, and edge cases
Disable Codex code review on the repository entirely
Treat every comment Codex produces as mandatory, without exception
cx-i3-code-review-with-codex.why: The lesson explicitly scopes review to correctness, security, and missed edge cases, and instructs Codex to skip style already covered by the linter to avoid noise.

cx-i3-code-review-with-codex.q: Why does the review prompt require a concrete 'why' for each flagged issue, not just a bare flag?
options: It's simply a formatting requirement enforced by GitHub
Comments lacking a stated reason are automatically deleted by Codex
It makes the pull request appear longer and more thorough
It's what lets you triage quickly - you can evaluate the reasoning instead of re-deriving whether the comment is even right
cx-i3-code-review-with-codex.why: A concrete explanation per comment turns triage into evaluating given reasoning rather than reverse-engineering whether the flagged issue is real.

cx-i3-code-review-with-codex.q: What's the risk of treating every automated Codex review comment as mandatory to fix?
options: There is no real risk - more fixes are always strictly better
Teams either drown in noise or learn to ignore the tool entirely; the actual skill is judgment about which comments matter
It guarantees the resulting code will ship with zero bugs
It eliminates the need for any human sign-off on the change
cx-i3-code-review-with-codex.why: The lesson frames Codex review as a second opinion, not a verdict - blanket compliance either overwhelms the team or trains them to dismiss the tool altogether.

cx-i4-landing-page-from-spec.q: Why does the landing page spec supply the literal headline, contact details, and CTA text instead of describing them in general terms?
options: It's simply good formatting practice with no functional effect
It prevents Codex from inventing a phone number, price, or testimonial that doesn't actually exist
Codex requires exact text or it will refuse the entire task
It reduces the file size of the generated HTML output
cx-i4-landing-page-from-spec.why: Supplying real content in the spec is what prevents Codex from fabricating facts - a real risk with an under-specified brief, as the lesson's example scenario illustrates.

cx-i4-landing-page-from-spec.q: The spec explicitly requires 'static HTML/CSS/JS only, no framework, no backend, no database' for a one-page open house site. Why include this constraint?
options: Static pages are the only kind of output Codex is technically capable of producing
It keeps the build proportional to a one-page brief instead of scaffolding infrastructure you don't need and can't maintain
Frameworks always load noticeably slower in every browser
It's a technical requirement for the mailto: link to function
cx-i4-landing-page-from-spec.why: Without this constraint, a vague brief risks an over-engineered setup with a framework and database for what should be a single HTML file.

cx-i4-landing-page-from-spec.q: Why is checking the page at a 375px mobile viewport part of the lesson's definition of done?
options: Most visitors to a page like an open house listing will actually view it on a phone
It's an arbitrary technical box to check with no real-world reason
375px is the only screen width any browser supports
It's optional and not actually part of the definition of done
cx-i4-landing-page-from-spec.why: The lesson highlights mobile-width verification specifically because most real visitors to this kind of page open it on a phone, so approving without checking is a listed common mistake.

cx-a1-cloud-tasks-vs-local.q: Which of these is the best fit for a Codex cloud task rather than a live local session?
options: Exploratory debugging of an unfamiliar production incident
A well-specified, bounded, lower-stakes task like a dependency bump or adding tests to an already-understood module
An ambiguous architecture decision with several open questions
Anything touching code you don't fully trust yet
cx-a1-cloud-tasks-vs-local.why: The lesson reserves cloud tasks for well-specified, bounded, lower-stakes work, while defaulting to local sessions for anything ambiguous, exploratory, or touching code you don't yet trust.

cx-a1-cloud-tasks-vs-local.q: Why do explicit constraints matter even more in a cloud-task spec than in a local session's spec?
options: They don't - constraints matter identically in both settings
Cloud tasks ignore any stated constraints by default
Cloud task billing scales with the number of constraints listed
There is no one present during an unsupervised cloud run to catch an overreach mid-task, so constraints are what prevent judgment calls you'd have vetoed live
cx-a1-cloud-tasks-vs-local.why: Cloud tasks run unsupervised, so constraints do more work than in a local back-and-forth session where you could interrupt and redirect in real time.

cx-a1-cloud-tasks-vs-local.q: A cloud task returns a pull request with all checks green. What should you do before merging?
options: Merge it directly from the GitHub UI since the checks already passed
Pull it down locally and run the full test suite yourself before merging
Trust the cloud environment's own report and skip local verification
Deploy the change to production immediately
cx-a1-cloud-tasks-vs-local.why: Merging a cloud-produced PR straight from GitHub without rerunning the suite locally is listed as a common mistake - the cloud claim is not proof.

cx-a2-tests-and-verification-habits.q: Codex reports 'all tests are passing' after a change. Per the lesson's core habit, what should you require?
options: Nothing further - a written claim from Codex is sufficient
A screenshot of a green checkmark
The actual test command and its full pasted output, not a summary
A verbal confirmation restated in the next chat message
cx-a2-tests-and-verification-habits.why: The lesson's rule is to never accept 'the tests pass' as a sentence - always require the actual command and its output, since a summary can be optimistic in a way raw output rarely is.

cx-a2-tests-and-verification-habits.q: Codex explicitly flags that it could not verify how a new discount badge renders visually. What's the correct next step?
options: Build a short manual verification checklist and check it yourself, since Codex can't literally see a rendered page
Ignore the flag since the automated tests already passed
Ask Codex to describe what it thinks the badge probably looks like
Skip visual verification entirely - it's rarely worth the time
cx-a2-tests-and-verification-habits.why: For anything Codex can't literally verify itself - visual layout, real API behavior, cross-browser rendering - the lesson calls for a manual checklist run by a human.

cx-a2-tests-and-verification-habits.q: Why does the verification prompt specifically ask whether any existing test was modified, and require a justification if so?
options: Modified tests are always evidence of improved coverage
It's purely a documentation nicety with no functional purpose
Existing tests can never legitimately be changed under any circumstance
It surfaces the failure mode where a suite goes green because an assertion was weakened rather than because the code was actually fixed
cx-a2-tests-and-verification-habits.why: This question is designed to catch the specific risk of a quietly loosened or skipped test making a failure disappear without the underlying bug being fixed.

cx-a3-delivery-workflow-end-to-end.q: Why does the end-to-end pipeline have Codex draft the PR description itself, tied to the spec's acceptance criteria?
options: It's purely to save the developer some typing time
It produces a reviewable artifact that explains intent for the next person, not just a diff with no stated reasoning
GitHub technically requires PR descriptions to be agent-generated
It replaces the need to write acceptance criteria in the original spec
cx-a3-delivery-workflow-end-to-end.why: A PR description mapped back to acceptance criteria turns the pull request into a reviewable artifact, rather than a diff a future reader has to reverse-engineer for intent.

cx-a3-delivery-workflow-end-to-end.q: After a change merges, where does the lesson say you should verify it actually works?
options: Nowhere further - passing test output is sufficient on its own
In the real running environment, not just in test output
Only by reviewing the CI logs a second time
Only in the PR's diff view on GitHub
cx-a3-delivery-workflow-end-to-end.why: The pipeline explicitly includes 'merge, then verify the change in the real running environment, not just in test output' as its own step.

cx-a3-delivery-workflow-end-to-end.q: A delivery reveals that Codex had to be told a convention or command it should already have known. What should happen?
options: Nothing - just re-explain it again the next time it comes up
Mention it once informally in a team chat message
Add it to AGENTS.md before moving on to the next task, so the pipeline improves over time
Keep it as unwritten, tribal knowledge among senior developers
cx-a3-delivery-workflow-end-to-end.why: The lesson treats AGENTS.md as a living document - each delivery is a chance to capture what had to be re-explained so it's never re-taught again.
